messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 31
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Carpenter
- Trauma Type: Police violence
- Pcl5: 42

He is a 31-year-old South Eastern Asian man who works as a carpenter, and much of his life before the trauma is organized around physical skill, routine, and responsibility. He takes pride in making things fit together cleanly, in measuring twice, in knowing that a frame will hold because he has done the work carefully. He is married, and in the years before the incident he is described as steady and practical, the kind of person who does not speak much about himself but shows care by coming home on time, bringing his wife small things she likes, and handling problems without complaint.

The trauma occurs during an encounter with police that escalates quickly and leaves him feeling powerless and confused. He does not expect to be treated as an enemy. In the moment, the experience is dominated by shouting, the sudden violence of being physically restrained, and the terrifying sense that what is happening is both real and impossible. Afterward, he finds it difficult to explain the event in a way that makes sense to anyone else, including himself. What stays with him most is not only the pain and fear, but the humiliation of being handled roughly and the conviction that he has lost control over his own body and safety. For someone who earns his living with his hands, the memory of being grabbed, pinned, and ordered around leaves a particular mark.

In the first weeks afterward, he tries to return to work as if nothing has changed. He shows up at the job site, carries lumber, and works the saw, but he is more easily startled and less able to settle into the rhythm that usually helps him think. A slammed truck door or a sharp voice makes his whole body tense before he can catch himself. He starts scanning for exits when he enters unfamiliar places, and he notices police cars immediately, even from a distance. His wife sees that he is more withdrawn at home. He sits through dinner with little appetite, says he is tired, and goes quiet when she asks how he is doing. At night, instead of sleeping deeply, he wakes with his chest tight and his mind already back at the scene, replaying pieces of it in fragments. Sometimes he lies still for a long time, listening to his breathing, trying to convince himself he is back in his own bedroom.

As the months pass, he begins to shape his life around avoiding reminders. He takes different routes when driving if he thinks he might pass the station where the police vehicles are parked. He does not want to watch news stories involving arrests or protests, and he turns away when the television shows uniforms, sirens, or someone being forced to the ground. If his wife mentions the incident or asks what he remembers, he becomes tense and short with her, not because he wants to be distant but because the questions pull him toward feelings he has worked hard to contain. He tells himself that thinking about it will only make him more angry and less useful at work. Still, the thoughts come anyway, often when he is idle and least prepared for them. He finds himself replaying what he could have done differently, then feeling ashamed that he could not protect himself better.

The anger does not stay neatly contained. At times he is irritable with co-workers over small mistakes, then feels guilty afterward and says little. He notices that he is more on guard around men in authority and that he reacts sharply when someone comes up behind him unexpectedly. He keeps his back to the wall in restaurants. He checks locks repeatedly before bed. In bed, he can be physically present with his wife but mentally elsewhere, caught in a loop of vigilance and dread that makes closeness harder. He loves her and wants to reassure her, yet he also feels embarrassed by how easily he is unsettled now. He worries that he seems weak, although people who know him see a man who is trying hard to keep functioning.

Even after some time has passed, the experience continues to shape the way he moves through the world. He remains committed to work, to his marriage, and to the practical tasks that give his days structure, but all of these require more effort now. He measures his reactions carefully, as if trying to build something stable from a foundation that no longer feels secure. What he carries most strongly is a sense that the event changed his relationship to safety: the world that once felt predictable now feels capable of turning violent without warning.
